changes.before: Low-Voltage GaN Utilization for High-Voltage Stacked Polyphase Bridge Inverter for Truck Propulsion
changes.after: Low-Voltage GaN Utilization in High-Voltage Stacked Polyphase Bridge Inverters for Truck Propulsion

changes.before: Abstract— The stacked polyphase bridge (SPB) partitions the dc-link voltage among series-connected submodules, enabling low-voltage gallium nitride (GaN) switches to be used in high-voltage traction drives. Its isolated machine winding sets also support continued operation following submodule bypass, distinguishing it from multilevel inverter topologies that require additional redundancy for fault tolerance. Realizing the favorable on-state resistance and switching characteristics of low-voltage GaN at traction-current levels, however, requires coordinated parasitic-aware design. This paper presents a phase-leg building block for a 300-kW, 1200-V SPB traction inverter. A charge-based device comparison motivates the selection of the 100-V EPC2361, while single-cell switching and loss assessments identify four parallel devices per switch position as a candidate for a sixteen-submodule configuration. Current-sharing sensitivity guides a symmetric arrangement of device pairs. An iterative KiCad–Ansys Q3D–LTspice workflow links the routed prototype, extracted parasitic network and switching response. With an estimated local commutation-loop inductance of 0.41 nH, optimization of the gate-drive settings achieves a simulated peak drain–source voltage of approximately 90 V while retaining fast switching at the assessed operating point. The results connect device-level selection to the physical constraints governing low-voltage GaN utilization in an SPB traction building block. Experimental validation of one building block is planned for the full paper.
changes.after: Abstract— The stacked polyphase bridge (SPB) partitions the dc-link voltage among series-connected submodules, enabling low-voltage gallium nitride (GaN) switches to be used in high-voltage truck propulsion systems. With suitable bypass hardware and winding control, its isolated machine winding sets also support continued operation following submodule bypass, unlike multilevel implementations without provisions for fault-tolerant operation. Realizing the favorable on-state resistance and switching characteristics of low-voltage GaN at the required phase-current levels, however, requires coordinated parasitic-aware design. This paper presents a phase-leg building block for a 300-kW, 1200-V SPB inverter for truck propulsion. A charge-based device comparison motivates the selection of the 100-V EPC2361, while single-cell switching and loss assessments identify four parallel devices per switch position as a candidate for a sixteen-submodule configuration. Current-sharing sensitivity guides a symmetric arrangement of device pairs. An iterative KiCad–Ansys Q3D–LTspice workflow links the routed prototype, extracted parasitic network and switching response. With an estimated local commutation-loop inductance of 0.41 nH and a 10-nH gate loop, revised gate-drive settings achieve a simulated peak drain–source voltage of 88.8 V and a 5.9-ns voltage fall time at 75 V and 322 A. A 5% bus-voltage increase exceeds the 90-V design target. The results connect device-level selection to the physical constraints governing low-voltage GaN utilization in an SPB truck propulsion building block. Experimental validation of one building block is planned for the full paper.

changes.before: High dc-link voltages support megawatt charging and traction power levels of several hundred kilowatts, but conventional two-level inverter switches must block the full dc-link voltage while conducting substantial phase current [1]. Multilevel converters enable the use of devices with lower blocking-voltage ratings, although the additional components introduce more potential failure points and do not automatically provide fault tolerance. The stacked polyphase bridge (SPB) connects three-phase bridges in series on the dc side, with each bridge supplying an isolated winding set of a common machine [2], [3]. This arrangement combines voltage partitioning with a modular structure that supports fault-tolerant operation. A faulty submodule can be bypassed while the remaining submodules and winding sets continue operating at reduced capability. Fig. 1 shows the voltage partitioning and the phase-leg building block considered here.
changes.after: High dc-link voltages support megawatt charging and truck propulsion power levels of several hundred kilowatts [1]. In propulsion operation, conventional two-level inverter switches must block the full dc-link voltage while conducting substantial phase current. Multilevel converters enable the use of devices with lower blocking-voltage ratings, although the additional components introduce more potential failure points and do not automatically provide fault tolerance. The stacked polyphase bridge (SPB) connects three-phase bridges in series on the dc side, with each bridge supplying an isolated winding set of a common machine [2], [3]. This arrangement combines voltage partitioning with a modular structure that supports fault-tolerant operation. With suitable bypass hardware and winding control, a faulty submodule can be bypassed while the remaining submodules and winding sets continue operating at reduced capability, subject to their voltage and current limits. Fig. 1 shows the voltage partitioning and the phase-leg building block considered here.

changes.before: Voltage partitioning enables each SPB submodule to use a lower semiconductor voltage class, creating an opportunity to exploit the favorable on-state resistance and switching characteristics of low-voltage gallium nitride (GaN) devices in high-voltage traction drives [4]. Increasing the submodule count reduces the voltage across each bridge but leaves the phase-current requirement unchanged for fixed total power, dc-link voltage, modulation index, and power factor. Several devices may therefore be required in parallel, making current sharing, gate-drive impedance, and commutation paths central to realizing the expected device benefits.
changes.after: Voltage partitioning enables each SPB submodule to use a lower semiconductor voltage class, creating an opportunity to exploit the favorable on-state resistance and switching characteristics of low-voltage gallium nitride (GaN) devices in high-voltage truck propulsion systems [4]. Increasing the submodule count reduces the voltage across each bridge but leaves the phase-current requirement unchanged for fixed total power, dc-link voltage, modulation index, and power factor. Several devices may therefore be required in parallel, making current sharing, gate-drive impedance, and commutation paths central to realizing the expected device benefits.

changes.before: Previous studies address SPB modulation and losses [3], dc-link stability [5], and comparisons with alternative GaN converter systems [6]. Research on paralleled GaN stages identifies complementary implementation constraints, including commutation inductance, source coupling, and unequal gate impedances [7]–[9]. These findings indicate that device-level comparisons must be complemented by an assessment of the routed building block: a favorable device figure of merit alone does not establish sufficient drain- and gate-voltage margins at traction current. Accordingly, this paper evaluates low-voltage GaN utilization by linking device selection, single-cell characterization, and parallel-count selection to a symmetric phase-leg implementation. A KiCad–Ansys Q3D–LTspice workflow connects the prototype layout to its parasitic network and switching response. The contribution is a quantitative assessment of how the power network and gate-drive settings jointly constrain the selection of the number of cells and the design of the SPB building block.  The introduction part will be extended in the final paper; the reduced version is given in the digest due to the page limitation.

changes.before: The selected EPC2361 is evaluated in a half-bridge model with one device per switch position. Inductive-load switching (uni-directional current) simulations are performed at a submodule voltage of 75 V over a device-current sweep. Gate-loop inductances of 10 nH and 20 nH represent the preliminary range of interest, while commutation-loop inductances of 0.5 nH and 1 nH represent a compact power path and a higher-inductance sensitivity case, respectively. Turn-on and turn-off gate resistances are fixed at 3 Ω and 1 Ω. The aim is to retain fast switching and low switching energy so that the device’s switching capability can be used effectively.
changes.after: The selected EPC2361 is evaluated in a half-bridge model with one device per switch position. Inductive-load switching (unidirectional current) simulations are performed at a submodule voltage of 75 V over a device-current sweep. Gate-loop inductances of 10 nH and 20 nH represent the preliminary range of interest, while commutation-loop inductances of 0.5 nH and 1 nH represent a compact power path and a higher-inductance sensitivity case, respectively. Turn-on and turn-off gate resistances are fixed at 3 Ω and 1 Ω. The manufacturer’s device model [10] uses 27 °C, −1/5-V gate commands, 0.85/0.35-Ω driver pull-up/down resistances, and 0.03-nH common-source inductance. Gate-loop values are assumed bounds, not extracted measurements. The aim is to retain fast switching and low switching energy so that the device’s switching capability can be used effectively.

changes.after: Fig. 3 separates the low-side drain–source voltage peak at turn-off from the high-side peak during low-side turn-on and reports both low-side switching energies. Voltage peaks cover the complete off interval and subsequent on interval. Near 80 A per device, the compact power path meets the drain-voltage target for both events, but the higher-inductance path does not. At lower current, the high-side peak can exceed the target even with the compact path, so the peak-current screen does not establish full-current-range feasibility. Increasing gate resistance can slow the relevant transition and reduce overshoot, but increases switching energy. Minimizing commutation inductance is therefore important for retaining voltage margin and the device’s switching-loss advantage. Because of the digest page limit, the full paper will expand the current-range assessment and simulation details.

changes.before: The single-cell switching-energy maps are evaluated over the sinusoidal phase-current waveform to estimate average switching losses. Because of the digest page limit, energy integration and the thermal model will be provided in the full paper.
changes.after: The single-cell switching-energy maps are evaluated over the sinusoidal phase-current waveform to estimate average switching losses. Turn-on energy is integrated over 150 ns and turn-off energy over the full 1-µs off interval to capture slow low-current capacitance charging. The first-pass cooling estimate assumes 7.62 K/W per device from junction to sink and 0.65 K/W from the shared phase-leg sink to 40 °C ambient. Loss accounting includes 10-ns dead time and a provisional 2.9-µJ capacitive freewheeling term per device per cycle. These assumptions require validation; the detailed model will be given in the full paper because of the digest page limit.

changes.after: Four parallel devices are retained as an initial implementation choice: this count meets the preliminary peak-current voltage screen with the compact commutation path. changes.before: The preliminary parallel-count choice assumes equal current sharing. Fig. 5(a) compares two parallel devices at 75 V and 120 A nominal total current, using 0/5 V gate commands, 3 Ω gate resistors, and nominal 10 nH gate loops. A power-loop mismatch of 0.1 nH produces approximately 8% peak-current imbalance; 10/15 nH gate loops produce approximately 56%; and removing the Kelvin return with a 0.05 nH source-inductance mismatch produces approximately 25%. The gate-loop mismatch is the most sensitive of these evaluated cases, motivating matched gate paths and dedicated Kelvin returns. Because of the digest page limit, the sensitivity analysis will be detailed in the full paper.
changes.after: The preliminary parallel-count choice assumes equal current sharing. Fig. 5(a) compares two parallel devices at 75 V and 120 A nominal total current, using 0/5 V gate commands, 3 Ω gate resistors, and nominal 10 nH gate loops. A power-loop mismatch of 0.1 nH produces approximately 2% peak-current imbalance; 10/15 nH gate loops produce approximately 17%; and removing the Kelvin return with a 0.05 nH source-inductance mismatch produces approximately 9%. Imbalance is 100|Ipk,1 − Ipk,2|/(Ipk,1 + Ipk,2), using each branch’s turn-on maximum. These different perturbations motivate matched gate paths and dedicated Kelvin returns, without establishing a universal sensitivity ranking. Because of the digest page limit, the sensitivity analysis will be detailed in the full paper.

changes.before: Connecting all four devices to one gate-driver output increases the total gate charge and the current required to establish the intended switching transition. The turn-off path must also sink the displacement current coupled through the gate–drain capacitance during drain-voltage transients. Excessive impedance in this path can cause a positive gate-voltage disturbance and reduce the margin against unintended turn-on. The four-device arrangement is divided into two device pairs per switch position. As illustrated in Fig. 5(b), each pair of switching cells is served by one dual-channel 2EDF7275K driver [10]. One channel drives two high-side GaNs and the other drives two low-side GaNs. The phase leg uses two drivers, with an individual gate resistor for each GaN.
changes.after: Connecting all four devices to one gate-driver output increases the total gate charge and the current required to establish the intended switching transition. The turn-off path must also sink the displacement current coupled through the gate–drain capacitance during drain-voltage transients. Excessive impedance in this path can cause a positive gate-voltage disturbance and reduce the margin against unintended turn-on. The four-device arrangement is divided into two device pairs per switch position. As illustrated in Fig. 5(b), each pair of switching cells is served by one dual-channel 2EDF7275K driver [11]. One channel drives two high-side devices and the other drives two low-side devices. The phase leg uses two drivers, with an individual gate resistor for each device.

changes.after: Fig. 7 shows a CAD rendering of the KiCad prototype board assembly and the Q3D conductor geometry. The estimated local commutation loop is approximately 0.41 nH per cell, including capacitor equivalent series inductance. The coupled power network contains 29 branches and 406 mutual terms, using dc resistance and partial inductances at 100 MHz. The scalar comprises 0.347 nH of copper and 0.062 nH of capacitor ESL at device/capacitor ports under equal branch excitation. Package and gate-path inductances were not separately extracted; gate loops remain assumed 10/20-nH bounds. This supports the compact-path assumption used for initial sizing. Because of the digest page limit, the full paper will detail layout and Q3D results.

changes.before: The prototype board results show that a compact power loop is necessary but does not by itself establish usable switching margin. Parallel count, branch symmetry, and gate-drive settings determine whether the selected voltage class remains practical. The higher gate-inductance case leaves no useful drain-voltage margin for tolerances or operating-point variation. If layout and drive changes cannot provide that margin, reducing the submodule voltage feeds back into the SPB series count. The lower gate-inductance case provides more headroom at this operating point, without establishing compliance over a complete traction operating envelope.
changes.after: The prototype board results show that a compact power loop is necessary but does not by itself establish usable switching margin. Parallel count, branch symmetry, and gate-drive settings determine whether the selected voltage class remains practical. The higher gate-inductance case leaves no useful drain-voltage margin for tolerances or operating-point variation. If layout and drive changes cannot provide that margin, reducing the submodule voltage feeds back into the SPB series count. With revised drive settings, the 10-nH case gives 88.0–88.8-V drain peaks at sampled nominal-current points; the 20-nH case reaches 91.8 V at lower current. At rated current, the 10-nH case has a 5.9-ns voltage fall time and 38.7-µJ summed low-side switching energy per device. Raising its local bus by 5% gives a 92.2-V peak, exceeding the target. The nominal result therefore does not establish the proposed voltage-variation allowance or compliance over a complete truck propulsion operating envelope. The 0.8-V reference is a minimum static threshold, not an absolute gate rating or proof against dynamic turn-on.
